title: Children in care in Northern Ireland reach record high, official figures show
standfirst: Department of Health statistics show 4,287 children were looked after in Northern Ireland at 31 March 2026, the highest since 1995, with 83 per cent living in foster care and more carers leaving than being approved.
body: The number of children in care in Northern Ireland has reached its highest level since the Children (Northern Ireland) Order 1995 came into force, according to the Department of Health's Children's Social Care Statistics for 2025/26, published on 15 October 2026. At 31 March 2026 there were 4,287 looked after children and young people.

Foster care remains by far the most common arrangement. The statistics show 83 per cent of looked after children were living in foster care, a share the department says is in line with previous years, with 7 per cent placed with their parents, 6 per cent in residential care and 4 per cent in other placements. During the year 1,038 children entered care and 900 left it.

The figures also give a picture of the fostering workforce. Health and Social Care Trusts had 2,821 approved foster carers at the year end, with a further 278 in the independent sector. Trusts carried out 641 initial home visits and completed 395 fostering assessments in 2025/26, while 329 trust-recruited carers de-registered during the year.

The Fostering Network said in May that Northern Ireland needs around 300 more foster carers, that the number of children entering care has risen by 46 per cent over ten years, and that carer numbers have fallen since 2021, citing finances, support and respect as reasons people leave. Allowances in Northern Ireland have not risen since 2024, according to the charity.

What this means for you: with fewer carers approved than de-registering, trusts continue to run regional appeals, including recent calls for short-break carers for disabled children. Anyone in Northern Ireland considering fostering can expect strong demand from their local trust. For existing carers, the record number of children in care underlines the pressure on placements and the case for better retention support.

title: Government launches England's first national foster carer recruitment drive
standfirst: The Department for Education has launched a nationally coordinated fostering recruitment campaign from Downing Street, aimed at people in their 30s and 40s, as part of its plan for 10,000 more foster places.
body: The Department for Education has launched what it describes as the first nationally coordinated foster carer recruitment campaign for England. It was unveiled at 10 Downing Street on 13 October 2026, at an event attended by foster carers, frontline staff and care-experienced people, and is being promoted through a dedicated government campaign website.

According to the DfE, the campaign is aimed mainly at adults in their 30s and 40s who have never seriously considered fostering. The department cites its own polling suggesting that around two thirds of people think they could foster if practical barriers were removed, and says approved foster carer numbers have fallen by 12 per cent while the number of children needing care has risen. The Fostering Network puts the decline at 63,890 carers in 2021 to 56,345 in 2025.

The campaign forms part of the reforms announced in February 2026, when the Children's Minister, Josh MacAlister, set out £88 million over two years and a target of 10,000 additional foster places by the end of this Parliament. The DfE says more than 70 per cent of councils are now part of a fostering hub, and its £12.4 million innovation fund is backing 11 programmes, including weekend fostering, parent-and-child placements and support for carers facing allegations.

The Fostering Network welcomed the campaign, which it said it had long called for, but its chief executive, Sarah Thomas, said recruitment alone is not enough and government must put equal effort into keeping existing carers and tackling the reasons they leave. Wales and Scotland have already run national campaigns, the charity noted.

What this means for you: councils in England are aligning local recruitment messages with the national campaign, and enquiries are increasingly routed through regional hubs rather than individual councils. Existing carers may see weekend and short-break roles piloted in their area. The announcement does not itself change allowances, tax relief or approval rules.

title: Eleven projects win Fostering Innovation Fund backing to trial new ways of fostering
standfirst: Regional recruitment hubs and care cooperatives will use a share of £12.4m to test weekend fostering, specialist remand placements, parent-and-child fostering and better support during allegations.
body: The Department for Education has named the 11 programmes sharing the £12.4 million Fostering Innovation Fund, in a document published on 14 October alongside the national recruitment campaign. The money covers 2026-27 and 2027-28 and includes evaluation costs.

Seven lead organisations are listed, all of them regional recruitment hubs or regional care cooperatives. Greater Manchester Combined Authority's cooperative leads four programmes: a housing solutions scheme with HOME, an expansion of its HIVE model, a specialist remand fostering programme and a transition pathway programme. Foster with North East is working with Now Foster on a 'weekenders' recruitment programme, and Fostering South West has two projects, one on recruitment, retention and training with the Black Foster Carers Alliance and one on support and training with Coram Leap.

The others are a specialist foster care hubs programme led by Foster4 Cheshire and Merseyside, therapeutic fostering training from Home and Future with the Mulberry Bush, a parent-and-child specialist fostering programme led by Local Community Fostering Greater London East with TACT and Somerset Council, and a carer retention programme focused on allegations, led by the London Regional Care Cooperative with The Fostering Network. Individual grant amounts and project descriptions have not been published.

The fund was trailed in February's Fostering Action Plan and opened in May, when the DfE said it wanted fostering models that fit modern households, a younger and more diverse carer base, and trials of respite and weekend-only fostering for children in residential or kinship care. Only cooperatives and council-run hubs could apply, with charity or independent partners.

What this means for you: if your fostering service sits in one of these regions, you may be offered new placement types, training or support over the next two years. London carers may see changes to how allegations are handled. The lead bodies are all council-led, so agency carers would be involved only through local partnerships.

title: First parts of Scotland's new foster care law come into force
standfirst: Provisions of the Children (Care, Care Experience and Services Planning) (Scotland) Act 2026 began on 30 September, including a power to make councils publish foster carer allowance and fee rates separately.
body: The first provisions of the Children (Care, Care Experience and Services Planning) (Scotland) Act 2026 came into force on 30 September 2026 under commencement regulations made by Scottish Ministers. Among them is section 36, which gives ministers the power to require councils, through regulations, to publish what they pay foster carers, broken down into allowances, fees and other payments.

The Act, passed on 19 March and given Royal Assent on 15 May 2026, is the main legislation for keeping the Promise. For fostering it allows ministers to set up a register of foster carers, starting with a pilot; requires fostering services to be charities; extends continuing care to a young person's 26th birthday; and lets eligible young people return to continuing care with their carer's agreement. Section 37 ties fostering and kinship allowance rates to the annual uprating mechanism in Scottish social security law.

Most of those provisions, including the register, the charity requirement and the uprating duty, were not switched on in September and need further regulations. The Fostering Network, which pressed for allowance and fee rates to be published separately, called the amendments a landmark step; its director for Scotland, Paul Sullivan, described them as life-changing for young people in foster care.

Implementation falls to a new minister. Siobhian Brown, Minister for Children, Young People and The Promise, recently met foster carers at a Fostering Network event in Edinburgh, where carers raised recognition, financial security and council support, and committed to seeing the Act's changes through.

What this means for you: nothing changes to payments yet. Once regulations are made under section 36, carers should be able to see their council's allowance and fee rates published separately and compare them. The Scottish Recommended Allowance rose by 3.8 per cent from April 2026, to £177.68 a week for under-fives, £206.71 for ages five to 15 and £283.35 for 16 and 17 year olds.

title: Ofsted plans five-point grades and a new carer-support judgement for fostering agencies
standfirst: Ofsted's consultation on overhauling children's social care inspection closed on 28 September. Independent fostering agencies face new grades, report cards and a judgement on how they recruit and support carers.
body: Ofsted's consultation on the biggest changes to children's social care inspection in several years closed on 28 September 2026. The proposals cover independent fostering agencies inspected under the social care common inspection framework (SCCIF) as well as council children's services, and Ofsted says it will publish its response in early 2027.

The central change is a move from the current four-point scale to five grades: exceptional, strong standard, expected standard, needs attention and urgent improvement. The overall judgement on children's experiences and progress would be dropped, with each evaluation area graded separately and reports published as online report cards with a colour-coded grid and an ungraded summary. Ofsted says the new grades would not be directly comparable with current ones.

For fostering agencies specifically, Ofsted proposes an additional evaluation area on the quality of foster carer recruitment, assessment and support, alongside a new area on children's enduring relationships that would apply to all settings. The three existing graded areas would remain. A needs attention grade in any area would bring the next inspection forward, and urgent improvement would be treated much as inadequate is today.

How often agencies are inspected is set by Department for Education regulations rather than by Ofsted, and dropping the overall judgement would require those regulations to change. Ofsted says SCCIF changes would be phased in between spring 2027 and spring 2028, with timing dependent on the DfE's wider reforms, including the new fostering standards awaiting a decision.

What this means for you: if adopted, your agency or council fostering service would be judged for the first time on how well it recruits, assesses and supports carers, and inspection reports would look very different. Carers may be asked for their views through the surveys Ofsted has introduced under SCCIF. Council children's services would move to a standard inspection every four years, with focused and monitoring visits in between.

title: Wales weighs ban on for-profit agencies approving new foster carers from 2027
standfirst: A Welsh Government consultation that closed on 23 September proposes that for-profit fostering services, which hold almost a quarter of fostering households in Wales, could not approve new carers from 1 April 2027.
body: A Welsh Government consultation on the next stage of removing profit from children's care closed on 23 September 2026. It proposes that from 1 April 2027 existing for-profit fostering services in Wales would no longer be able to approve new foster carers, and for-profit children's homes could not add beds.

The proposals implement the Health and Social Care (Wales) Act 2025. Since 1 April 2026, Care Inspectorate Wales has been unable to register new for-profit fostering services, children's homes or secure accommodation, and councils have had a strengthened duty to prioritise local authority and not-for-profit placements. In a written statement on 8 July, the Deputy Minister for Social Care, Delyth Jewell, said currently approved carers and existing placements would not be affected by the 2027 restriction.

The consultation also asked about transitional arrangements to let carer approvals carry over when a for-profit agency re-establishes itself as a not-for-profit body and registers with CIW, where there is clear organisational continuity. The Welsh Government's third progress report, published in July, shows 16 for-profit fostering agencies in Wales at 31 March 2026 with 811 fostering households, 23 per cent of the total, compared with 162 households in not-for-profit agencies and 2,507 with local authorities.

Separately, councils must submit draft placement sufficiency plans to Welsh Ministers by 1 December 2026, with approved plans published by 31 March 2027. The next progress report, with data to 30 September 2026, is expected later this year.

What this means for you: carers approved by a for-profit agency in Wales keep their approval and placements, but from April 2027 their agency could not take on new carers unless it converts to a permitted not-for-profit form such as a charity or community interest company. Prospective carers in Wales are likely to find councils, working together as Foster Wales, and not-for-profit agencies are the main routes in.

title: Scottish minister hears foster carers' call for recognition and financial security
standfirst: Foster carers told Siobhian Brown, the recently appointed Minister for Children, Young People and The Promise, that respect, money and council support are their priorities, at a Fostering Network event in Edinburgh.
body: The Fostering Network brought foster carers together with Siobhian Brown, Scotland's new Minister for Children, Young People and The Promise, at an informal event in Edinburgh, the charity reported on 21 September. Much of the session was small-group conversation about carers' day-to-day experiences and what they want to change.

Three themes dominated, according to the charity: greater recognition and respect for carers, financial security, and more support from local authorities. The minister committed to upholding The Promise, Scotland's reform programme for care-experienced children and young people, and to seeing through the changes made by the Children (Care, Care Experience and Services Planning) (Scotland) Act 2026. Several of the carers present sit on the charity's Foster Carer Advisory Board and plan to keep engaging with her during this Parliament.

The meeting comes against a backdrop of falling capacity. The Care Inspectorate's latest fostering bulletin, summarised by CELCIS, recorded 2,828 fostering households in Scotland at the end of 2024, down 5.7 per cent on the year, with 3,680 children in foster care against 3,918 a year earlier. When the Scottish Government launched its national recruitment campaign in May 2025, The Fostering Network estimated Scotland needed at least 400 more carers and was losing more than 350 a year.

Some councils have moved on pay. In May, City of Edinburgh Council replaced age-banded fees with a single weekly fee of £307.50 for mainstream carers, an increase it put at around 60 per cent for those caring for under-12s, paid on top of the Scottish Recommended Allowance, which rose 3.8 per cent this year.

What this means for you: the charity says it wants more opportunities for carers to speak directly to the minister and to officials, with its advisory board the main route. The 2026 Act and The Promise set the framework for any changes to allowances, support and recognition, so it is worth following your council's and the charity's updates on implementation.

title: Charities urge automatic free school meals for every child in care in England
standfirst: The Fostering Network and TACT say half of foster carers surveyed expected children in their care to lose free school meals under eligibility rules that changed in September 2026.
body: The Fostering Network and TACT have launched a campaign calling on the government to give every child in care in England an automatic entitlement to free school meals, warning that eligibility changes from September 2026 could leave many foster children losing out.

From this school year, free school meals in England are available to all children in households receiving Universal Credit, replacing the previous £7,400 earnings threshold. Children in care have never been automatically entitled: eligibility depends on whether the carer's household receives a qualifying benefit. Transitional protection from 2018, which let children who qualified before entering care keep their meals, ran only until the end of 2025/26, according to Suffolk County Council's fostering service.

A survey of 713 foster carers in England by the two charities found that 51 per cent expected children in their care to lose free school meals from September. Around a third of foster carers are of pensionable age, and those who do not claim Universal Credit, for example because they have retirement savings, cannot pass on entitlement to the children they look after. Many said the loss could exceed £100 per child a month and would also end access to the Holiday Activities and Food programme.

Eight organisations, including the two charities, the Nationwide Association of Fostering Providers, CoramBAAF, Adoption UK, Foster Talk, BASW and Home for Good, have written to the Education Secretary and the Children's Minister, Josh MacAlister, asking for automatic entitlement, continued access to linked schemes and clear guidance for schools, councils and fostering services. No government response had been published at the time of writing.

What this means for you: if a child you foster has lost free school meals this term, the decision turns on your household's benefit status rather than the child's needs. Carers on Universal Credit can apply through their council; under current rules others cannot. Schools still receive pupil premium plus for looked after children regardless.

title: Plan to replace 31 fostering standards with seven awaits government response
standfirst: A DfE consultation on rewriting England's fostering standards and guidance closed on 16 September. The government's response, due this autumn, will shape how every fostering service is run and inspected.
body: A Department for Education consultation on rewriting the national standards and statutory guidance for fostering services in England closed on 16 September 2026, with the government's response promised for the autumn. The ten-week consultation, launched on 8 July, is a main plank of the department's Renewing Fostering action plan.

Under the proposals, the 31 Fostering Services National Minimum Standards from 2011 would be replaced by seven outcome-focused Quality Standards, and the current Training, Support and Development Standards would become seven Foster Carer Development Standards covering a carer's first year after approval. The DfE says the rewrite would cut more than 185 pages of guidance to around 80, folding the Children Act 1989 Volume 4 guidance and the 2013 assessment and approval guidance into one document.

The draft also proposes a dedicated standard on allegations, separating them from standards-of-care concerns and expecting services to keep paying carers during investigations; tougher requirements for panel chairs, who would need at least three years' post-qualifying social work experience; and a 28-day window in which carers who give notice to resign could withdraw it. The consultation document cites 4,690 mainstream fostering households deregistering in 2024/25 as part of its case for change.

The Fostering Network welcomed the draft as a shift to a more relational approach, with carers treated as equal partners and given more delegated authority over everyday decisions. Its director for England, James Copeland, said the charity wants fees paid for 52 weeks a year, stronger guidance on the police role in allegations and more investment in Staying Put.

What this means for you: the new standards would apply to every council fostering service and independent agency in England, and Ofsted is revising its inspection framework to align with them. Nothing changes until the final version is issued. The DfE's implementation plan lists the standards for updating from autumn 2026 and says the national minimum allowance and tax relief will also be reviewed.

title: National Care Leavers' Month returns in November with a focus on empowerment
standfirst: The Alliance for Children in Care and Care Leavers is running the second month-long celebration of care-experienced people in November 2026, with free online workshops and a social media drive.
body: National Care Leavers' Month runs throughout November 2026 under the theme 'Leading the Way: From Experience to Empowerment', according to Become, the charity for children in care and young care leavers and a member of the organising Alliance for Children in Care and Care Leavers. The month celebrates the achievements of care-experienced people and aims to raise awareness of the issues they face among the public, professionals, carers and decision-makers.

Become is hosting free online sessions for care-experienced young people on Wednesdays through the month: young people's rights on 4 November, a policy and employment crossover with its Propel into Work programme on 11 November, UCAS applications on 18 November and wellbeing at university on 25 November. It is also asking care-experienced people to share an achievement they never expected to reach, using the #NCLM hashtag, and offers social media templates for supporters.

The month-long format is still new. The event was known as National Care Leavers' Week until 2025, when a planning group of professionals and care-experienced people linked to the Alliance extended it to a full month, after care-experienced people said one week was too short to recognise their successes and press the issues that still need attention, according to the National Leaving Care Benchmarking Forum, which announced the change in May 2025.

For 2026 Become's page sets out no specific asks of councils, employers or foster carers, concentrating instead on encouraging supporters to learn about the care system and amplify care leavers' own stories.

What this means for you: foster carers supporting young people approaching or past 18 may want to pass on the workshops, particularly the sessions on rights and university applications. Fostering services, councils and agencies often run local events for care leavers and Staying Put households during the month, so it is worth checking what your own service has planned.
